claim: Diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs) are aggressive and fatal pediatric tumors of the central nervous system that are highly resistant to treatments.
source: Diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs) are aggressive and fatal pediatric tumors of the central nervous system that are highly resistant to treatments.
evidence: This is a general characterization of DMGs supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: Lysine to methionine substitution of residue 27 on histone H3 (H3-K27M) is a driver mutation in DMGs.
source: Lysine to methionine substitution of residue 27 on histone H3 (H3-K27M) is a driver mutation in DMGs, reshaping the epigenetic landscape of these cells to promote tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature on DMG mutations.

claim: H3-K27M gliomas are characterized by deregulation of histone acetylation and methylation pathways.
source: H3-K27M gliomas are characterized by deregulation of histone acetylation and methylation pathways, as well as the oncogenic MYC pathway.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction and background literature.

claim: H3-K27M gliomas are characterized by deregulation of the oncogenic MYC pathway.
source: H3-K27M gliomas are characterized by deregulation of histone acetylation and methylation pathways, as well as the oncogenic MYC pathway.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction and background literature.

claim: Treatment of H3-K27M patient-derived cells with Sulfopin in combination with Vorinostat resulted in substantial decrease in cell viability.
source: Treatment of H3-K27M patient-derived cells with Sulfopin, an inhibitor shown to block MYC-driven tumors in vivo, in combination with the HDAC inhibitor Vorinostat, resulted in substantial decrease in cell viability.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 2).

claim: Sulfopin is an inhibitor shown to block MYC-driven tumors in vivo.
source: Treatment of H3-K27M patient-derived cells with Sulfopin, an inhibitor shown to block MYC-driven tumors in vivo, in combination with the HDAC inhibitor Vorinostat, resulted in substantial decrease in cell viability.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dubiella et al., 2021.

claim: Transcriptome and epigenome profiling revealed synergistic effect of Sulfopin and Vorinostat combination in downregulation of prominent oncogenic pathways such as mTOR.
source: Moreover, transcriptome and epigenome profiling revealed synergistic effect of this drug combination in downregulation of prominent oncogenic pathways such as mTOR.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and Cut&Run data presented in the manuscript (Figure 2).

claim: In vivo studies of patient-derived orthotopic xenograft models showed significant tumor growth reduction in mice treated with the drug combination.
source: Finally, in vivo studies of patient-derived orthotopic xenograft models showed significant tumor growth reduction in mice treated with the drug combination.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo bioluminescence imaging data (Figure 4).

claim: Up to 80% of diagnosed DMG children exhibit a lysine 27 to methionine (H3-K27M) mutation in one of the genes encoding histone H3.3 and H3.1.
source: Sequencing studies showed that up to 80% of the diagnosed children exhibit a lysine 27 to methionine (H3-K27M) mutation in one of the genes encoding histone H3.3 and H3.1 (clinically classified as DMG, H3 K27M-mutant).
evidence: This is supported by citations to sequencing studies.

claim: H3-K27M mutation drives pronounced alterations in the epigenetic landscape.
source: Numerous subsequent studies revealed pronounced alterations in the epigenetic landscape driven by this histone mutation (Castel et al., 2015; Fontebasso et al., 2014; Schwartzentruber et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Global epigenetic alterations in H3-K27M DMGs include a drastic loss of H3 lysine 27 tri-methylation (H3K27me3).
source: Among these global epigenetic alterations are a drastic loss of H3 lysine 27 tri-methylation (H3K27me3), concomitant with an increase in H3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27ac).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Global epigenetic alterations in H3-K27M DMGs include an increase in H3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27ac).
source: Among these global epigenetic alterations are a drastic loss of H3 lysine 27 tri-methylation (H3K27me3), concomitant with an increase in H3 lysine 27 acetylation (H3K27ac).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Epigenetic alterations in H3-K27M DMGs affect transcriptional programs and support tumorigenesis.
source: These epigenetic alterations were shown to affect transcriptional programs and support tumorigenesis (Bender et al., 2013; Chan et al., 2013; Lewis et al., 2013; Krug et al., 2019; Piunti et al., 2017; Harpaz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: Pan-histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi), such as Vorinostat and Panobinostat, were found to inhibit growth of H3-K27M malignant gliomas.
source: Indeed, pan-histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi), such as Vorinostat and Panobinostat, were found to inhibit growth and to restore gene expression alterations observed in H3-K27M malignant gliomas (Grasso et al., 2015; Yin et al., 2007; Su et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: H3-K27M cells develop resistance to HDACi treatment.
source: However, recent studies demonstrated that H3-K27M cells develop resistance to HDACi treatment (Grasso et al., 2015; Su et al., 2022), stressing the importance of identifying novel drug combinations to induce synergistic inhibition of oncogenic pathways.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: High-level gene amplification of MYC is recurrently observed in pediatric high-grade gliomas.
source: High-level gene amplification of MYC is recurrently observed in pediatric high-grade gliomas (Buczkowicz et al., 2014; Mackay et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: H3-K27M gliomas show high expression of MYC and MYC target genes.
source: H3-K27M gliomas show high expression of MYC and MYC target genes, due to both epigenetic alterations and structural variants, resulting in a viability dependency on MYC signaling (Krug et al., 2019; Pajovic et al., 2020; Dubois et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Sulfopin is a PIN1 inhibitor that downregulates MYC target genes in vitro.
source: The PIN1 inhibitor, Sulfopin, was shown to downregulate MYC target genes in vitro and to block MYC-driven tumors in murine models of neuroblastoma (Dubiella et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dubiella et al., 2021.

claim: Sulfopin blocks MYC-driven tumors in murine models of neuroblastoma.
source: The PIN1 inhibitor, Sulfopin, was shown to downregulate MYC target genes in vitro and to block MYC-driven tumors in murine models of neuroblastoma (Dubiella et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dubiella et al., 2021.

claim: RNA sequencing analysis of H3-K27M-mutant patient-derived glioma cells (SU-DIPG13) treated with Sulfopin revealed strong enrichment of MYC targets among the downregulated genes.
source: Indeed, RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis of H3-K27M-mutant patient-derived glioma cells (SU-DIPG13) treated with Sulfopin revealed strong enrichment of MYC targets among the downregulated genes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: Genes downregulated by Sulfopin were enriched for MYC-bound genes identified in several non-glioma cell lines.
source: The genes downregulated by Sulfopin were also enriched for MYC-bound genes identified in several non-glioma cell lines, supporting a role for PIN1 in activation of the MYC pathway also in these glioma cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Sulfopin did not lead to PIN1 degradation.
source: Of note, Sulfopin was developed as a covalent inhibitor of PIN1, and did not lead to PIN1 degradation, as previously shown (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Dubiella et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and citation to Dubiella et al., 2021.

claim: Cut&Run analysis revealed an increase in H3K27me3 levels around the transcriptional start sites (TSS) of MYC target genes upon Sulfopin treatment.
source: Interestingly, Cut&Run analysis (Skene and Henikoff, 2017) revealed an increase in H3K27me3 levels, indicative of repressed chromatin (Ferrari et al., 2014), around the transcriptional start sites (TSS) of MYC target genes, correlating with silencing of these genes upon PIN1 inhibition (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by Cut&Run data presented in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Global H3K27me3 distribution on all TSS and gene body regions was not affected by Sulfopin treatment.
source: Of note, global H3K27me3 distribution on all TSS and gene body regions was not affected by Sulfopin treatment, supporting a specific increase in H3K27me3 on the TSS of MYC target genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This is supported by Cut&Run data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and G.

claim: Sulfopin-unique H3K27me3 peaks were enriched for MYC target genes.
source: Furthermore, Sulfopin-unique H3K27me3 peaks (i.e. peaks that were found only in the Sulfopin-treated cells, and not in DMSO-treated cells) were enriched for MYC target genes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis of Cut&Run data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Sulfopin treatment led to a mild reduction in cell viability in all H3-K27M glioma cultures tested.
source: In line with downregulation of MYC signaling, Sulfopin treatment led to a mild reduction in cell viability, conserved across the different cultures (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: H3-K27M-mutant cells show higher sensitivity to Sulfopin treatment compared to H3-K27M knockout cells.
source: In both lines, the reduction in cell viability was partially rescued in the KO cells (Figure 1F), suggesting higher sensitivity of H3-K27M-mutant cells to MYC inhibition by Sulfopin.
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data in isogenic cell lines presented in Figure 1F.

claim: DMG cells showed greater sensitivity to Sulfopin compared to human astrocytic-like cells.
source: Of note, DMG cells showed greater sensitivity to the inhibitor compared to human astrocytic-like cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: DMG samples showed significantly higher expression of MYC and its target genes compared to normal samples.
source: Interestingly, while DMG samples showed significantly higher expression of MYC and its target genes compared to normal samples, PIN1 expression was lower in the cancer compared to matched normal tissue (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–K).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published transcriptomic data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–K.

claim: PIN1 expression was lower in DMG samples compared to matched normal tissue.
source: Interestingly, while DMG samples showed significantly higher expression of MYC and its target genes compared to normal samples, PIN1 expression was lower in the cancer compared to matched normal tissue (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–K).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published transcriptomic data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–K.

claim: H3-K27M-mutant tumors showed higher expression of MYC compared to H3 WT tumors.
source: Furthermore, H3-K27M-mutant tumors showed higher expression of MYC, compared to H3 WT tumors, while PIN1 levels were reduced across samples (Mackay et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 1L and M).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1L and M.

claim: The response to Sulfopin treatment (as reflected by IC50 measurements) correlated with the cells' doubling time.
source: The response to Sulfopin treatment (as reflected by IC50 measurements) correlated with the cells' doubling time (Figure 1—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1N.

claim: MYC levels negatively correlated with the IC50 of Sulfopin.
source: Indeed, MYC levels negatively correlated with the IC50 of Sulfopin; thus, cells relaying on high MYC activity showed higher sensitivity to Sulfopin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1P).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1P.

claim: Sulfopin treatment resulted in reduction of H3K27me3 signal over CpG islands.
source: Interestingly, Sulfopin treatment resulted in reduction of H3K27me3 signal over CGIs, perhaps contributing to Sulfopin-dependent growth inhibition in these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1Q).
evidence: This is supported by Cut&Run data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1Q.

claim: The combination of Sulfopin and Vorinostat had the strongest effect on cell viability, reducing viability by 80%.
source: We found that the combination of Sulfopin and Vorinostat (HDACi) had the strongest effect, reducing viability by 80% (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: An additive effect of Sulfopin and Vorinostat was detected in all the H3.3-K27M DMG cultures in most of the drug doses.
source: Moreover, while an additive effect of Sulfopin and Vorinostat was detected in all the H3.3-K27M DMG cultures in most of the drug doses, for the H3.1-K27M cultures we measured an additive effect only in higher dosages of Vorinostat (Figure 2C–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by BLISS index calculations presented in Figure 2C–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: H3.1- and H3.3-K27M cells differed substantially in MYC expression levels, with H3.1-K27M cells expressing significantly lower levels of MYC.
source: In line with the difference in sensitivity, H3.1- and H3.3-K27M cells differed substantially in MYC expression levels, with H3.1-K27M cells expressing significantly lower levels of MYC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claim: BLISS indexes negatively correlated with MYC expression levels.
source: Indeed, BLISS indexes negatively correlated with MYC expression levels (Figure 2F), indicating that H3.3-K27M cells, which express higher levels of MYC, are more sensitive to the combination of Sulfopin and Vorinostat.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis presented in Figure 2F.

claim: A total of 494 genes were significantly differentially expressed in cells treated with the drug combination, compared to only 145 and 167 in cells treated solely with Sulfopin or Vorinostat, respectively.
source: A total of 494 genes were significantly differentially expressed (DE) in cells treated with the drug combination, compared to only 145 and 167 in cells treated solely with Sulfopin or Vorinostat, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1K and L).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1K and L.

claim: The mTORC1 signaling pathway was significantly enriched in downregulated genes following the combined treatment.
source: Importantly, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed that this pathway was significantly enriched in downregulated genes following the combined treatment (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis presented in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1O.

claim: Additional epigenetic and oncogenic pathways such as BMI1, cAMP, and IL-6/JAK/STAT3 were significantly downregulated in cells treated with the drug combination.
source: Of note, additional epigenetic and oncogenic pathways such as BMI1, cAMP, and IL-6/JAK/STAT3 were significantly downregulated in cells treated with the drug combination (Abdouh et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2020; West et al., 2018; Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis presented in Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1O.

claim: The combined treatment with Sulfopin and Vorinostat led to induction of p21 (CDKN1A).
source: Importantly, we also confirmed that the combined treatment with Sulfopin and Vorinostat led to induction of p21 (CDKN1A), a prominent tumor suppressor promoting cell cycle arrest and regulated by mTOR signaling (Shamloo and Usluer, 2019; Tahmasebi et al., 2014; Cui et al., 2021; Figure 2H and J).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and western blot data presented in Figure 2H and J.

claim: mTOR expression in all the tested DMG cultures revealed a strong negative correlation with the BLISS indexes of the combined treatment.
source: Finally, exploring mTOR expression in all the tested DMG cultures revealed a strong negative correlation with the BLISS indexes of the combined treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1Q), suggesting mTOR as a potential biomarker of response for the combined treatment of Sulfopin and Vorinostat.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1Q.

claim: Global quantification by single-molecule measurements of H3K27-acetylated nucleosomes confirmed HDACi-mediated increase in H3K27ac global levels.
source: Indeed, global quantification by single-molecule measurements of H3K27-acetylated nucleosomes, as well as western blot analysis, confirmed HDACi-mediated increase in H3K27ac global levels (Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule imaging and western blot data presented in Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment with Sulfopin alone reduced the percentage of acetylated nucleosomes.
source: Interestingly, treatment with Sulfopin alone had the opposite effect, reducing the percentage of acetylated nucleosomes (Figure 3B and C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule imaging and western blot data presented in Figure 3B and C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The global HDACi-mediated increase in histone acetylation was attenuated in the combined treatment with Sulfopin.
source: As a result, the global HDACi-mediated increase in histone acetylation was also attenuated in the combined treatment with Sulfopin (Figure 3B and C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule imaging and western blot data presented in Figure 3B and C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The combined treatment led to the strongest local reduction of H3K27ac levels associated with cluster 1 gene promoters.
source: Moreover, in accordance with the reduction in RNA expression levels of genes comprising cluster 1, the combined treatment led to the strongest local reduction of H3K27ac levels associated with their promoters (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by Cut&Run data presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Cluster 1 genes gained H3K27me3 on their promoters upon the combined treatment.
source: Cluster 1 genes also gained H3K27me3 on their promoters upon the combined treatment, supporting their epigenetic repression following Sulfopin and Vorinostat treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by Cut&Run data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Genes associated with Vorinostat-unique enhancers were strongly enriched for oncogenic pathways such as RAS, MAPK, and PI3K-AKT signaling pathways.
source: Importantly, genes associated with these enhancers were strongly enriched for oncogenic pathways such as RAS, MAPK, and PI3K-AKT signaling pathways (Fernández-Medarde and Santos, 2011; Braicu et al., 2019; Rascio et al., 2021; Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by enrichment analysis of Cut&Run data presented in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Treatment of H3-K27M DMG xenograft mice models with the drug combination led to reduced tumor growth.
source: In line with our in vitro results, we found significant reduction in tumor growth following the combined treatment compared to control DMSO-treated mice (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo bioluminescence imaging data presented in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The combined treatment significantly reduced the fraction of H3-K27M cells that are positive to mTOR signal.
source: The combined treatment significantly reduced the fraction of the double-positive cells, compared to DMSO (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 4C and D.

claim: mTOR signal in the mouse cells surrounding the tumor showed no significant differences between the DMSO and the combination-treated mice.
source: Of note, mTOR signal in the mouse cells surrounding the tumor showed no significant differences between the DMSO and the combination-treated mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence staining data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The standard of care for H3-K27M-mutant DMGs remains solely radiation, with no significant improvement in overall survival.
source: Despite decades of efforts to improve treatment for children diagnosed with H3-K27M-mutant DMGs, the standard of care remains solely radiation, with no significant improvement in overall survival (Johung and Monje, 2017; Hayden et al., 2021; Nagaraja et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Ongoing clinical trials revealed preliminary evidence of clinical benefit for HDAC inhibition in DMGs.
source: High-throughput drug screens in patient-derived cells identified HDAC inhibition as a promising therapeutic strategy, and ongoing clinical trials revealed preliminary evidence of clinical benefit (Lin et al., 2019; Cooney et al., 2018) (NCT02717455, NCT03566199).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies and clinical trial identifiers.

claim: Emerging resistance to HDACi in glioma cells highlights the necessity to discover additional therapy modalities.
source: However, emerging resistance to HDACi in glioma cells (Grasso et al., 2015), as well as limited therapeutic benefits of HDACi treatment as a sole agent (Hennika et al., 2017; Leszczynska et al., 2021), highlight the necessity to discover additional therapy modalities that could prolong survival and relieve symptoms.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: High MYC activity is correlated with poor prognosis in H3-K27M-mutant DMGs.
source: In H3-K27M-mutant DMGs, as well as in many other malignancies, high MYC activity is correlated with poor prognosis and therefore considered as an attractive therapeutic target (Buczkowicz et al., 2014; Oster et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Direct targeting of MYC is highly challenging, functional, and structural wise.
source: Nevertheless, direct targeting of MYC is highly challenging, functional, and structural wise.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: MYC signaling, while amplified in cancer cells, is also essential to normal cell function.
source: MYC signaling, while amplified in cancer cells, is also essential to normal cell function (Pelengaris et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: As a transcription factor, MYC lacks traditionally druggable binding pockets.
source: Moreover, as a transcription factor, MYC lacks traditionally druggable binding pockets, hindering the development of direct small molecule binders (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Preclinical studies have shown in vivo activity and negligible toxicity of Sulfopin in murine models of PDAC and neuroblastoma.
source: Preclinical studies have shown in vivo activity and negligible toxicity of Sulfopin in murine models of PDAC and neuroblastoma (Dubiella et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dubiella et al., 2021.

claim: PIN1 is not overexpressed in DMG tumors.
source: While PIN1 is not overexpressed in DMG tumors, we show that Sulfopin, although not inhibiting MYC directly, downregulates MYC target genes in patient-derived DMG cells and affects cell survival in an H3-K27M-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of published transcriptomic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Despite a significant reduction in tumor size in vivo, the combined treatment did not increase mice survival.
source: Notably, despite a significant reduction in tumor size in vivo, the combined treatment did not increase mice survival.
evidence: This is based on the in vivo experimental results described in the manuscript.

claim: AKT gain or PTEN loss is detected in approximately 70% of DMG tumors.
source: Specifically, AKT gain or PTEN loss is detected in approximately 70% of DMG tumors, and a recent study showed high expression of mTOR in DMGs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The PTEN/AKT/mTOR pathway is suggested to play a key role in DMG disease.
source: Thus, the PTEN/AKT/mTOR pathway is suggested to play a key role in this disease (Warren et al., 2012; Panditharatna et al., 2015; Zarghooni et al., 2010; Tsoli et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: First-generation mTOR inhibitors primarily inhibited mTORC1, which often caused upregulation of mTORC2.
source: Attempts to restrict mTOR signaling using first-generation mTOR inhibitors primarily inhibited mTORC1, which often caused upregulation of mTORC2 (Guertin and Sabatini, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Drug agents targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2 were shown to be highly effective in DMG cells as well as in murine models.
source: Of note, drug agents targeting both mTORC1 and mTORC2 were shown to be highly effective in DMG cells as well as in murine models (Miyahara et al., 2017; Flannery et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Expression of the H3-K27M oncohistone is associated with a prominent increase in H3K27ac levels.
source: Expression of the H3-K27M oncohistone is associated with a prominent increase in H3K27ac levels (Lewis et al., 2013; Krug et al., 2019; Piunti et al., 2017; Furth et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Among the loci that accumulate H3K27ac are repetitive elements and endogenous retroviruses, resulting in their aberrant expression.
source: Among the loci that accumulate this modification are repetitive elements and endogenous retroviruses, resulting in their aberrant expression, potentially inducing innate immune responses (Krug et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Krug et al., 2019.

claim: H3-K27M cells do not show an increase in interferon stimulated genes (ISGs), presumably due to high levels of MYC.
source: However, H3-K27M cells do not show an increase in interferon stimulated genes (ISGs), preassembly due to high levels of MYC, which is potent antagonist of interferon responses (Krug et al., 2019; Schlee et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The high levels of H3K27ac in H3-K27M cells was linked to activation of super-enhancers, which regulate the expression of oncogenes and genes that are associated with an undifferentiated state.
source: The high levels of H3K27ac in H3-K27M cells was also linked to activation of super-enhancers, which regulate the expression of oncogenes and genes that are associated with an undifferentiated state (Nagaraja et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nagaraja et al., 2017.

claim: MYC overexpression results in H3K27ac gain on super-enhancers.
source: This Sulfopin-mediated attenuation could potentially result from downregulation of MYC targets, as it was recently shown that MYC overexpression results in H3K27ac gain on super-enhancers (See et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to See et al., 2022.

claim: Cells that divide faster were more sensitive to Sulfopin treatment.
source: The response to Sulfopin treatment (as reflected by IC50 measurements) correlated with the cells' doubling time (Figure 1—figure supplement 1N). Cells that divide faster were more sensitive to Sulfopin treatment, in line with PIN1 role in regulating cell cycle progression, and specifically G2/M transition (Yeh and Means, 2007; Pinch et al., 2020).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between doubling time and IC50, combined with knowledge about PIN1's role in cell cycle.

claim: MYC levels may predict the response to Sulfopin.
source: As expected, the doubling time negatively correlated with MYC expression, suggesting that MYC levels may predict the response to Sulfopin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1O).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between MYC expression and doubling time, and the correlation between doubling time and Sulfopin response.

claim: MYC and MYC target genes are potential biomarkers of response for the combined treatment.
source: Importantly, this highlights MYC, and MYC target genes, as potential biomarkers of response for the combined treatment.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between MYC expression and BLISS indexes.

claim: mTOR is a potential biomarker of response for the combined treatment of Sulfopin and Vorinostat.
source: Finally, exploring mTOR expression in all the tested DMG cultures revealed a strong negative correlation with the BLISS indexes of the combined treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1Q), suggesting mTOR as a potential biomarker of response for the combined treatment of Sulfopin and Vorinostat.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between mTOR expression and BLISS indexes.

claim: Dual targeting of both HDAC and MYC pathways has the potential of inducing robust expression of ISGs, thus promoting tumor cell death mediated by viral mimicry.
source: Thus, dual targeting of both HDAC and MYC pathways has the potential of inducing robust expression of ISGs, thus promoting tumor cell death mediated by viral mimicry (Jones et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the known effects of HDAC inhibition and MYC inhibition.

claim: The rapid deterioration of mice is likely a result of the aggressiveness of the transplanted tumors and does not represent side effects of the treatment.
source: This rapid deterioration is likely a result of the aggressiveness of the transplanted tumors and does not represent side effects of the treatment, as mice from all groups, including the non-treated mice, showed similar signs of deterioration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all groups showed similar deterioration.

claim: The combined treatment with Sulfopin and Vorinostat led to robust inhibition of several target proteins in the mTOR signaling pathway, likely via alternative pathways.
source: The combined treatment with Sulfopin and Vorinostat led to robust inhibition of several target proteins in the mTOR signaling pathway, likely via alternative pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed downregulation of mTOR pathway components without direct mTOR inhibition.

claim: One potential mechanism for mTOR pathway inhibition is the mTOR-dependent cell growth through MYC regulation, which may be impaired by Sulfopin treatment.
source: One potential candidate is the mTOR-dependent cell growth through MYC regulation, which may be impaired by Sulfopin treatment, inhibiting MYC transcriptional activity (Zoncu et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2009; Sodi et al., 2015; Kuo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism inferred from known interactions between MYC and mTOR pathways.

claim: Sulfopin-mediated attenuation of H3K27ac accumulation could potentially result from downregulation of MYC targets.
source: This Sulfopin-mediated attenuation could potentially result from downregulation of MYC targets, as it was recently shown that MYC overexpression results in H3K27ac gain on super-enhancers (See et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism inferred from the observed effects and published literature.
